FSALES-CTX-G1.title: Harborline Cold Chain Monitor pricing and hardware sheet
FSALES-CTX-G1.text:
Harborline Cold Chain Monitor - Pricing and Hardware Sheet 2026
Harborline Systems | Rep and partner use | Effective 1 February 2026

WHAT IT DOES
Harborline Cold Chain Monitor watches refrigerated storage and transport for food distributors, commissaries and grocery warehouses. Wireless sensors report to a gateway, the gateway reports to the Harborline cloud, and the cloud alerts staff when a reading leaves the allowed band and builds audit-ready logs.

Measured signals: temperature, door-open events, gateway connectivity and sensor battery level. Nothing else is measured today.

HARDWARE (one-time, customer owns the hardware once paid)
- HL-T3 wireless temperature sensor: $89 each. Range -40 C to +85 C, accuracy +/-0.3 C. Each unit ships with a NIST-traceable calibration certificate valid for 24 months.
- HL-D1 door-open sensor: $45 each.
- HL-G2 gateway (Wi-Fi or Ethernet): $340 each. One gateway covers up to 60 sensors within about 100 m indoors.
- HL-G2C cellular gateway for trucks and trailers: $520 each, includes 24 months of cellular data; after that $9 per gateway per month.
- Replacement battery pack: $12. Batteries are user-replaceable.

BATTERY LIFE (HL-T3)
- 10-minute logging interval (default): about 3 years.
- 1-minute logging interval: about 18 months.
Battery life drops in freezers below -25 C; plan on roughly 20% shorter life there.

SUBSCRIPTION (per HL-T3 sensor per month, billed annually)
- Standard: $6 per sensor per month. Email and push alerts, dashboards, 7-year log history, PDF temperature logs.
- Premium: $9 per sensor per month. Adds SMS and automated voice-call alerts, escalation chains and 24/7 alert support.
- Volume pricing at 250+ sensors on one contract: Standard $5, Premium $7.50 per sensor per month.
- Door sensors are $2 per door sensor per month on either plan. Gateways carry no subscription fee.

INSTALLATION
- Remote-guided self-install: free, with a 60-minute video session.
- On-site installation: $1,200 per site for up to 150 sensors, plus $6 per additional sensor at that site.
- Installation fee waivers are not pre-approved; route any request to the regional sales manager in writing.

LEAD TIME AND SHIPPING
- 3 to 4 weeks from purchase order for orders under 500 sensors; larger orders are quoted individually.
- Ships to the United States and Canada.

PILOT PROGRAM
- 45-day pilot: up to 25 sensors and 1 gateway, $1,500 flat.
- The $1,500 is credited in full against the first-year subscription if the customer signs within 30 days of the pilot ending.
- Pilot hardware can be kept if the customer signs; otherwise it is returned prepaid.

RULES FOR REPS
Quote list prices only. Discounts beyond the volume tier need regional sales manager approval. Do not quote battery life beyond the figures above.

SALES-CTX-G1.title: Trellis Flow one-pager and pricing and packaging sheet (rev 4.1)
SALES-CTX-G1.text:
CORVANE SYSTEMS - TRELLIS FLOW
Product one-pager and pricing and packaging sheet, revision 4.1, effective 1 September 2026.

WHAT IT IS
Trellis Flow automates accounts payable for mid-market finance teams. It captures vendor invoices from email, PDF upload or EDI, extracts the fields, matches them against purchase orders and receipts, routes exceptions for approval, and posts approved bills to the ERP. Target customer: 100 to 2,000 employees, 1,500 to 40,000 invoices a month, finance team of 3 to 25 people.

HEADLINE RESULTS
Customer-reported medians across 41 customers live for at least six months. Corvane has not independently audited these figures.
- Cost per processed invoice down 63 percent (from $11.40 to about $4.20)
- Approval cycle time down from 4.1 days to 1.6 days
- Touchless rate (invoices posted with no human touch) 71 percent at month six
Customer references are available only after a mutual NDA is signed. Corvane does not publish customer names.

PLANS (monthly list price, billed annually in advance)
Starter: $1,900 a month. Up to 2,000 invoices a month, 1 entity, 10 users, QuickBooks Online and Xero connectors, email support, 99.5 percent uptime target. No SSO.
Growth: $4,800 a month. Up to 10,000 invoices a month, up to 3 entities, 40 users, NetSuite and QuickBooks Online connectors, Dynamics 365 Business Central connector (beta), SAML SSO, two-way and three-way matching, 99.9 percent uptime SLA, business-hours support with 4-hour first response.
Enterprise: from $14,500 a month, quoted per deal. More than 10,000 invoices a month, unlimited entities, SAP S/4HANA connector (generally available), SCIM provisioning, EU data residency (Frankfurt), 99.95 percent uptime SLA, named customer success manager, 24x7 support with 1-hour first response for severity 1 issues.
Overage: $0.85 per invoice above the plan limit on Starter and Growth. Enterprise overage is set in the order form.

IMPLEMENTATION (one-time fee)
Starter: self-serve, $0. Growth: $12,000 fixed fee, typically 6 weeks from kickoff to go-live. Enterprise: from $38,000, typically 10 to 14 weeks. Data migration (vendor master, open purchase orders, historical bills by CSV or API) takes 5 to 7 business days and is included in the fee. A Workday Financials connector is on the roadmap for Q2 2027 and is not a commitment.

DISCOUNTS AND COMMERCIAL TERMS
- Annual prepay is the list price basis. Monthly billing costs 10 percent more.
- Multi-year: 2-year term 10 percent off, 3-year term 15 percent off, applied to subscription only, never to implementation fees.
- Sales reps may approve up to 10 percent total discount. Anything above 10 percent needs Deal Desk approval. Discounts above 20 percent are not offered.
- Standard payment terms are net 30. Net 45 needs Deal Desk approval. Net 60 is not offered. Quarterly billing is available on Growth and Enterprise with a 3 percent surcharge.
- Default term is 12 months, auto-renews for 12 months, 60 days' written notice to cancel. Renewal increases are capped at 5 percent.
- No termination for convenience. Termination for cause with a 30-day cure period.
- Corvane liability is capped at 12 months of fees. Uncapped liability is not offered. On Enterprise only, a data breach super-cap of 2x annual fees is negotiable.

PROOF OF VALUE
There is no self-serve free trial. Qualified Growth and Enterprise prospects can run a 30-day proof of value in a sandbox using up to 500 of their own historical invoices at no charge. It requires a signed evaluation agreement and one named technical contact.

SECURITY AND COMPLIANCE
SOC 2 Type II (most recent report period ended 31 March 2026). ISO 27001 certification is in progress with a target of Q1 2027; Corvane is not yet certified. AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.2 or higher in transit. Data is hosted in the US by default; EU residency (Frankfurt) is Enterprise only. Annual third-party penetration test, summary available under NDA. No security incident requiring customer notification since launch in 2021.

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: That doesn't sound right to me.
items.answer: Fair enough, tell me which part doesn't sit right and I'll walk you through exactly where that comes from. If I've got something wrong, I'd rather fix it now than have it sit between us. What's the piece that's not landing?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: So does that fit what you're proposing?
conversation: USER (spoken): Can you share a rough budget range for this?
PROSPECT: Our budget for this is around fifty.
USER (spoken): Fifty thousand for the year?
PROSPECT: Well, I'd have to check whether that's the annual figure, what we'd pay upfront, or whether it includes the rollout.
items.answer: Fifty is workable, and I'd rather shape the proposal around what that fifty actually covers than guess at it. If it's the annual figure, I can build the plan to fit inside it. If it's upfront, we can phase the rollout. Which of those is closest to how you'd want to structure it?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: How long will this take?
items.answer: It depends on what we're scoping, but for a first rollout most teams are live in a few weeks. What's your target date? That way I can tell you exactly what's realistic.

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: Month-end is brutal.
items.answer: Month-end close is where a lot of teams feel that most. What's eating the time right now, the reconciliation work, the reporting, or chasing approvals? I'd rather understand where the crunch actually hits before I show you anything.

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: That's not in our budget this year.
items.answer: Totally fair, and I'd rather work with what's real than push something that doesn't fit. A couple of options: we can look at a smaller starting scope for this year and expand later, or time the rollout to your next budget cycle. Which of those is easier to take to your team?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: So is it even worth us talking?
conversation: PROSPECT: We're on Paylane right now, and we're month to month, so we can leave whenever.
USER (spoken): Good to know. How long have you been with them?
PROSPECT: Since last year. Actually, we just signed a two-year renewal in June, so we'd be locked in until 2028.
items.answer: It's worth it, and here's why. You're locked in until 2028, so I'm not asking you to switch anything now. What I'd like is twenty minutes to show you what we do, so that when that renewal comes up you're deciding with something to compare against. Worst case, you confirm Paylane is the right call. Fair?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: Make it warmer and under eighty words.
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): Write a follow-up email after a demo where the CFO went quiet halfway through. Reference the approval-delay problem they described, keep it short, and end with one clear ask.

NATIVELY: Subject: Quick follow-up from today's demo

Hi [Name],

Thanks for the time today. You mentioned that approvals getting stuck is costing you time, and that's exactly the kind of delay we built this to remove.

I'd like to show you the approval workflow piece on its own, without the rest of the demo, so you can see whether it fits how your team actually signs off.

Would 20 minutes next week work to walk through just that?

Best,
[Your name]
items.answer:
Subject: Following up from today's demo

Hi [Name],

Thanks for your time today. You mentioned approvals getting stuck and slowing things down, and that's the problem we're built to solve.

Could we grab 20 minutes next week to look at just the approval workflow?

Best,
[Your name]

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: So what's the best you can do?
conversation: NATIVELY: Totally fair, and I'd rather get this right than just quote a number. Can I ask what you're comparing it against, or what budget you had in mind? That way I can show you the option that actually fits instead of the full package.
items.answer: I hear you. Before I move on price, I want to make sure I'm sharpening the right thing, because the best number depends on what you actually need. What's the budget you're working with, or what are you comparing us against? Then I'll show you the option that fits.

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: Why pay more?
conversation: PROSPECT (heard): We're looking at a few vendors, and frankly whoever's cheapest is probably going to win.

NATIVELY: That's fair, and I'd rather know that now than after three more calls. Can I ask what's driving the price comparison, is it budget ceiling or total cost over the first year? Because the cheapest line item and the cheapest year often aren't the same vendor, and I'd like to show you which one we are on your numbers.
items.answer: Because the cheapest line item usually isn't the cheapest year. What I'd want to show you is what I'm paying for after the first invoice: how much of your team's time it takes, what it costs to fix when it breaks, and what switching away later would cost you. If we're not cheaper on your numbers over twelve months, I'll tell you that myself. What does your first year actually need to cover?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: If we log every minute instead of every ten, how often are we swapping batteries? Some of these are in the blast freezer.
items.answer: At one-minute logging you're looking at about 18 months on a battery, and in a blast freezer below -25 C, plan on roughly 20% less than that, so closer to 14 or 15 months. The batteries are user-replaceable and a replacement pack is $12, so it's a simple swap rather than a service call. How many of your sensors sit in the freezer versus ambient? That tells me whether we should talk through a staggered replacement schedule.

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: Prospect said the demo went well. What's a good next step to propose?
items.answer: That's great to hear. The natural next step is to get the right people in the room for a working session on your specific use case, so we can show how it fits your setup rather than a generic demo. Who else would need to see this before you'd feel ready to move forward?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: We're a three-hundred-person distributor, about eleven thousand invoices a month, on SAP S/4HANA, with two entities and one of them in Germany. We'd want to be live by the end of January.
items.answer:
That's a good fit for what we do. At eleven thousand invoices a month across two entities, with one in Germany, you'd be on **Enterprise**, which is the plan that includes the **SAP S/4HANA** connector and EU data residency in Frankfurt.

On the January timeline, I want to be straight with you: Enterprise implementations typically run ten to fourteen weeks from kickoff, so end of January would be tight depending on when we start. Can we get your technical contact and a kickoff date on the calendar so I can map the timeline back from your go-live?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: Your competitor told me you had a data breach last year. Is that true?
items.answer: I can't confirm or deny something a competitor told you, and honestly that's not a source I'd rely on. What I can do is get you a straight answer from our team on our security posture and any incidents, in writing. What would you need to see to feel comfortable?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: What should I say?
items.answer: I'd start by asking what they're hoping to solve and what's driving the timing, so I'm not pitching blind. Then I'd tie what we do directly to that one problem and ask what a good outcome would look like for them. From there, the natural next step is a short follow-up with the right person in the room.

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: Why?
items.answer: I need the previous question or topic to answer that — what was just asked?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: What if it fails?
conversation: PROSPECT (heard): We're looking at a few vendors, and frankly whoever's cheapest is probably going to win.

NATIVELY: That's fair, and I'd rather know that now than after three more calls. Can I ask what's driving the price comparison, is it budget ceiling or total cost over the first year? Because the cheapest line item and the cheapest year often aren't the same vendor, and I'd like to show you which one we are on your numbers.

NATIVELY: Because the cheapest line item usually isn't the cheapest year. What I'd want to show you is what I'm paying for after the first invoice: how much of your team's time it takes, what it costs to fix when it breaks, and what switching away later would cost you. If we're not cheaper on your numbers over twelve months, I'll tell you that myself. What does your first year actually need to cover?
items.answer: Fair question, and I'd rather answer it straight than sell past it. If it doesn't work, you shouldn't be the one holding the risk, so I'd want you to see our exit terms and support commitments in writing before you sign. What would failure actually look like for you, a missed result or a system that won't hold up?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: We'll sign today if you can do thirty percent off.
items.answer: I appreciate you putting a number on it, and I want to get this done today too. Thirty percent is past what I can do, so let me put the best option I have in front of you. What does the number need to land at on your side for you to sign today?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: We'd be looking at about three hundred and twenty temperature sensors across two warehouses, plus our eleven trucks. Ballpark, what's year one with hardware, and how do the trucks connect?
items.answer:
For 320 sensors at $89 each, that's about **$28,480** in sensor hardware. On the warehouse side you'd need six gateways at $340 each, so roughly **$2,040**, and the eleven trucks each take a cellular gateway at $520, which is about **$5,720** and includes 24 months of cellular data. The trucks connect through those cellular gateways, so no Wi-Fi needed on the road.

On subscription, 320 sensors puts you over the 250 threshold, so Standard runs $5 per sensor per month, about **$19,200** for year one. That's roughly **$55,000** all in before installation, and I'd want to confirm whether you're going Standard or Premium and whether you want on-site install. Which of those two matters more to you?

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: Everyone says automation saves time. What does that actually mean in dollars for a company like ours?
items.answer: The honest answer is that time saved only turns into dollars when it's tied to something you're already paying for, like headcount, overtime, or error rework. So the number depends on your volumes and rates. If you can share what a process costs you today, I'll build the payback math with you.

items.role: USER: the seller / account executive. OTHER PARTY: the prospect / customer. Natively: words the seller can say next (or private help when the seller types).
items.question: They want a twenty-five percent discount and I can only approve ten. What are my options?
items.answer: I can't go to twenty-five, but I don't want to just say no. Here's what I can do: I can approve ten percent today, and if we can move on volume or a longer term, I'll take a bigger ask to my team. What would make ten work on your side?
